{{Short description|British statistician}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Dorothy''' '''Enid Charles''' (29 December 1894 – 26 March 1972) was a British [[socialist]], [[feminist]] and [[statistician]] who was a pioneer in the fields of [[demography]] and [[population statistics]].

She was born in [[Denbigh]], [[Wales]]. She obtained a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[mathematics]], [[economics]] and [[statistics]] at [[Newnham College, Cambridge]], where she became friends with Dorothy (Dodo) Crowther, sister of the writer [[James Crowther]].<ref name="Hill-Andrews">{{cite book |last1=Hill-Andrews |first1=Oliver |title=Interpreting Science J G Crowther and the Making of British Inter-War Culture |date=2015 |publisher=University of Sussex |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/42579223.pdf}}</ref> She gained a Ph.D. in [[physiology]] from the [[University of Cape Town]], South Africa.<ref name=SW>{{citation|year=2005 |author=Sylvia Wargon |title=Legacy of Enid Charles, 1894–1972 |journal=Canadian Studies in Population |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=137–153 |doi=10.25336/P62K5C |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Charles met the [[conscientious objector]] [[Lancelot Hogben]] while at Cambridge; they married in 1918.<ref name=TimesObit>{{citation | title = Dr. Enid Charles | newspaper = [[The Times]] | date = April 3, 1972}}</ref> Out of a dozen or so socialist and feminist couples in Britain in the early 20th century, Charles was the only wife to keep her name.<ref>{{citation | author1 = Outram, Dorinda | author2 = Abir-Am, Pnina G. |author2-link=Pnina Abir-Am| title = Uneasy Careers and Intimate Lives: Women in Science, 1789–1979 | publisher = Rutgers University Press | location = New Brunswick, N.J | year = 1987 | isbn = 0-8135-1256-5 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/uneasycareersint00sbio }}</ref>  The couple, who had two sons and two daughters,<ref name=www>{{cite book|title=Who Was Who, 1971-1980|year=1981|publisher=A and C Black|page=[https://archive.org/details/whowaswho197119800lond/page/375 375]|isbn=0-7136-2176-1|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/whowaswho197119800lond/page/375}}Sketch on Lancelot Hogben.</ref> separated in 1953 and divorced in 1957.<ref name=odnb>{{cite book|title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Volume 27|year=2004|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=0-19-861377-6}}Article on Hogben by Robert Bud.</ref>

Charles worked on [[Total fertility rate|fertility rates]] and marriage rates for the [[Statistics Canada|Dominion Bureau of Statistics]] in [[Canada]]. In 1934, Charles projected drastic decline in population of the United Kingdom if fertility rates continued to fall. These results led her to speak out against the then commonly accepted principle of [[eugenics]].<ref>{{citation|year=1996 |author=W.H.G. Armytage |title=The Social Context of Eugenic Thought |publisher=[[Galton Institute]] |url=http://www.galtoninstitute.org.uk/Newsletters/GINL9606/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121103739/http://www.galtoninstitute.org.uk/Newsletters/GINL9606/index.html |archive-date=2008-11-21 }}</ref><ref>{{citation | year = 1993 | author = Pedersen, Susan | author-link = Susan Pedersen (historian) | title = Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State in Britain and France, 1914–1945 | publisher = Cambridge University Press | location = Cambridge, UK | isbn = 0-521-55834-4}}</ref> She subsequently worked as a Regional Adviser in Epidemiology and Health Statistics and as a Population Statistics Consultant for the [[World Health Organization]] in [[Singapore]] and [[New Delhi]].<ref name=SW/>

She died in [[Torquay]], England, in 1972, aged 77.<ref name=TimesObit/>
